qr.q: For what value of k does the equation x^2 + 6x + k = 0 have exactly one real solution?
qr.why: Fastest: a perfect square: x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2 has the single root -3, so k = 9. Full method: one real solution means the discriminant is zero: b^2 - 4ac = 36 - 4(1)(k) = 0, so k = 9. Takeaway: discriminant positive, two real roots; zero, one; negative, none. For x^2 + bx + k, one root means k = (b/2)^2.

qr.q: What are all the solutions of 2x^2 - 18 = 0?
qr.why: Fastest: 2x^2 = 18, so x^2 = 9 and x = 3 or -3. Full method: Step 1, add 18: 2x^2 = 18. Step 2, divide by 2: x^2 = 9. Step 3, take both square roots: x = 3 or x = -3. (Factoring agrees: 2(x - 3)(x + 3) = 0.) Takeaway: isolate x^2 completely, then remember both the positive and negative roots.

qr.q: What is the sum of the solutions of x^2 + 5x - 14 = 0?
qr.why: Fastest: for x^2 + bx + c, the roots add to -b: here -5. Full method: factor: (x + 7)(x - 2) = 0, so x = -7 or x = 2. Sum = -5. (Their product is -14, the constant term.) Takeaway: the roots of x^2 + bx + c add to -b and multiply to c.

qr.q: A lab orders 19 boxes of gloves, and each box holds 98 gloves. About how many gloves is that?
qr.why: Fastest: round the near-hundred: 98 is about 100, so 19 x 100 = 1,900. (Exactly 19 x 98 = 1,862.) Full method: 19 x 98 = 19 x (100 - 2) = 1,900 - 38 = 1,862, and the closest choice is 1,900. Takeaway: round to friendly numbers, and keep track of the zeros; choices on the DAT are often a factor of 10 apart.

qr.q: A pump moves 706 liters of water per hour. About how many liters does it move in 46 hours?
qr.why: Fastest: 700 x 46 = 7 x 46 x 100 = 322 x 100 = 32,200, closest to 32,000. (Exactly 706 x 46 = 32,476.) Full method: round 706 to 700 and multiply: 32,200; the choice nearest the exact 32,476 is 32,000. Takeaway: round only the number that is close to a friendly value, and count zeros before you pick.

qr.q: A clinic network performs 2,192 cleanings per week. About how many cleanings does it perform in 69 weeks?
qr.why: Fastest: 2,200 x 70 = 154,000, so about 150,000. (Exactly 2,192 x 69 = 151,248.) Full method: round both factors to friendly numbers near them, 2,200 and 70; their product, 154,000, sits closest to 150,000, and the exact product 151,248 confirms it. Takeaway: round each factor to its nearest friendly value, then check that no other choice is closer.

Fastest: add x and add 9 in one move: 3x = 19, so x = 19/3 (about 6.33). Full method: Step 1, add x to both sides: 3x - 9 = 10. Step 2, add 9: 3x = 19. Step 3, divide by 3: x = 19/3. Check: 2(19/3) - 9 = 11/3 and -19/3 + 10 = 11/3. Takeaway: a term changes sign when it crosses the equals sign; keep the answer as a fraction until the end.

Fastest: subtract x and 8 in one move: 3x = -3 - 8 = -11, so x = -11/3 (about -3.67). Full method: Step 1, subtract x: 3x + 8 = -3. Step 2, subtract 8: 3x = -11. Step 3, divide: x = -11/3. Check: 4(-11/3) + 8 = -20/3 and -11/3 - 3 = -20/3. Takeaway: collect x on the side with the larger coefficient, and carry the sign all the way through.

qr.q: Events A and B have P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.2, and P(A and B) = 0.01. What is P(A or B)?
qr.why: Fastest: or = add, minus the overlap: 0.3 + 0.2 - 0.01 = 0.49. Full method: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). The overlap is inside both P(A) and P(B), so it is subtracted once: 0.49. Takeaway: OR adds and then removes the double-counted overlap; AND is the overlap itself.

qr.q: A clinic sees 40 patients per day. The daily count rises 25 percent, and then the new count falls 20 percent. How many patients per day does the clinic see now?
qr.why: Fastest: 1.25 x 0.8 = 1, so the count is back to 40. Full method: Step 1, up 25 percent: 40 x 1.25 = 50. Step 2, down 20 percent of 50, which is 10: 50 - 10 = 40. Takeaway: successive percents multiply; a 25 percent rise and a 20 percent fall exactly undo each other because 1.25 x 0.8 = 1.

qr.q: A tank holds 4,000 liters of water. A drain removes 7 liters per minute while a pipe adds 3 liters per minute. Starting full, how many minutes will it take for the tank to empty?
qr.why: Fastest: net loss is 7 - 3 = 4 liters per minute, so 4,000 / 4 = 1,000 minutes. Full method: rate out minus rate in = 4 L/min. Time = amount / net rate = 4,000 / 4 = 1,000 minutes. Takeaway: opposing rates subtract; then time = amount / net rate.

qr.q: If 3^(2x - 1) = 27, what is the value of x?
qr.why: Fastest: 27 = 3^3, so the exponents match: 2x - 1 = 3 and x = 2. Full method: Step 1, write both sides with base 3: 3^(2x - 1) = 3^3. Step 2, equal bases mean equal exponents: 2x - 1 = 3. Step 3, x = 2. Check: 3^3 = 27. Takeaway: rewrite both sides with the same base, then set the exponents equal.

qr.q: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours. Pipe B fills the same tank in 9 hours. Pipe C empties the tank in 12 hours. If all three pipes are open simultaneously, how long does it take to fill the empty tank?
qr.why: Fastest: use a 36-unit tank. A adds 6 units per hour, B adds 4, C removes 3: net 7 units per hour, so 36/7 hours (about 5.1). Full method: net rate = 1/6 + 1/9 - 1/12 = 6/36 + 4/36 - 3/36 = 7/36 tank per hour. Time = 36/7 hours. Takeaway: fillers add rates, drains subtract them; then flip the net rate to get the time.

qr.q: A solution that is 25% acid by volume is mixed with a solution that is 60% acid. To produce 35 liters of a final solution that is 40% acid, how many liters of the 25% solution must be used?
qr.why: Fastest: seesaw. 40 is 15 from 25 and 20 from 60, so 25-percent : 60-percent = 20 : 15 = 4 : 3. 4/7 of 35 = 20 L. Full method: let x be liters of 25 percent; 35 - x is liters of 60 percent. Acid: 0.25x + 0.60(35 - x) = 0.40(35) = 14. So 21 - 0.35x = 14, giving x = 20 L. Takeaway: the larger share sits closer to the target strength; check it with the acid equation.

qr.q: In a dataset of 7 numbers, the mean is 12 and the median is 10. Each number is increased by 5. What are the new mean and median?
qr.why: Fastest: adding a constant slides the whole data set, so every center moves by that constant: 17 and 15. Full method: new mean = (sum + 7 x 5) / 7 = old mean + 5 = 17. The order of the values does not change, so the middle value also rises by 5: 15. Takeaway: adding c shifts mean, median and mode by c and leaves the spread alone; multiplying by c scales all of them.

gc.q: A platinum catalyst is added to the gas-phase decomposition 2 H2O2(aq) -> 2 H2O(l) + O2(g) at 298 K, dramatically speeding up the reaction without being consumed. Considering the Arrhenius equation k = A·exp(−Ea/RT), which thermodynamic/kinetic parameter does a catalyst directly affect?
gc.why: A catalyst lowers E_a by providing an alternative reaction path with a lower transition-state barrier. ΔH, ΔG, ΔS, and K_eq are state functions and are unchanged by a catalyst.

gc.q: The polarity of a covalent bond is set by the electronegativity difference ΔEN. Pauling values: H = 2.1, F = 4.0, Cl = 3.0, Br = 2.8, I = 2.5. Calculate ΔEN for each H-X bond and identify the MOST polar.
gc.why: ΔEN values: H-F = 1.9, H-Cl = 0.9, H-Br = 0.7, H-I = 0.4. Largest ΔEN = most polar bond, so H-F is the most polar. Within the halide series, polarity decreases down the group as halogen EN drops.

gc.q: A chemistry student dissolves four reagents separately in dry, aprotic dichloromethane at 25°C: HCl, BF3, NH3, and OH-. They then test each for the ability to accept an electron pair (Lewis acid) versus the ability to donate a proton (Bronsted acid). Which species behaves as a Lewis acid yet has NO ionizable proton to donate, making it Bronsted-inactive?
gc.why: BF3 has an empty 2p orbital on boron and accepts an electron pair, fulfilling the Lewis-acid definition. It has no H to release, so it cannot be a Bronsted acid. HCl is both a Bronsted and Lewis acid, while NH3 and OH- are bases.

gc.q: Molten Al2O3 (cryolite-dissolved) is electrolyzed in a Hall-Heroult cell. The cathode reaction is Al^3+ + 3 e- -> Al(s), with M(Al) = 27 g/mol and F = 96485 C/mol. A total charge of 9650 C passes through the cell. Calculate the mass of aluminum deposited.
gc.why: Moles e- = 9650/96485 = 0.100 mol. Moles Al = 0.100/3 = 0.0333 mol. Mass = 0.0333 x 27 = 0.90 g. Forgetting to divide by n = 3 gives the trap value 2.7 g.

gc.q: Equal moles of Ne, Ar, Kr, and Xe are placed in separate flasks at the same temperature, 298 K. The kinetic theory of gases gives average translational kinetic energy as KE_avg = (3/2)kT per molecule, depending only on T. Which sample has the highest average KE per molecule?
opts: All four are equal because T is the same
gc.why: Average KE = (3/2)kT depends ONLY on temperature, not mass. At identical T, all four gases have the same average KE per molecule. Lighter Ne moves FASTER (higher v_rms) but with the SAME average KE, since KE = ½mv² and m·v² is conserved across species at equal T.

gc.q: In an operating galvanic cell at 25 °C, electrons flow externally from anode to cathode, while ions flow through the salt bridge to maintain electrical neutrality in each half-cell. Cations from the salt-bridge electrolyte (e.g., K+) migrate to balance charge buildup. In which direction do these cations move?
gc.why: At the cathode, reduction consumes positive ions (e.g., Cu^(2+) -> Cu), creating a buildup of negative charge. Cations from the salt bridge flow toward the cathode to neutralize this; anions flow to the anode.

gc.q: Water (H₂O, MW = 18) is a liquid at room temperature, while hydrogen sulfide (H₂S, MW = 34) is a gas, even though H₂S is heavier and would seem to have stronger London forces. What is the underlying reason for this anomaly?
opts: H₂O can form strong O-H···O hydrogen bonds; H₂S cannot (S is too large/less electronegative)
H₂S and H₂O have different volumes
H₂O is a metal but H₂S is not
H₂S has more electrons so more London force
gc.why: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F. Sulfur is below this electronegativity threshold and too large for the focused dipole. H₂O has extensive H-bonding (raising BP to 100°C); H₂S has only weak dipole-dipole forces (BP -60°C, hence a gas at RT).

gc.q: An equilibrium mixture of N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g) sits in a sealed 5.00 L vessel at 500 K. A chemist injects 1.0 mol of inert argon while keeping the volume constant at 5.00 L. Considering that K_p depends only on partial pressures of N2, H2, and NH3 (not on Ar), which way does the equilibrium shift?
gc.why: Adding inert gas at constant V does not change the partial pressures or molar concentrations of N2, H2, or NH3, so Q is unchanged and Q = K still holds. Le Chatelier's principle predicts no shift. (At constant pressure, dilution would shift toward more moles of gas.)

gc.q: In the same Haber problem (1.00 mol N₂ limiting; 4.5 mol H₂ initially), N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ uses 3 mol H₂ per 1 mol N₂. After complete reaction, how many moles of H₂ remain UNREACTED?
gc.why: H₂ consumed = 3 × 1.00 = 3.0 mol. H₂ remaining = 4.5 − 3.0 = 1.5 mol. Forgetting the 3:1 ratio gives 3.5 mol; subtracting the wrong way gives a negative or 0.5 result.

gc.q: Ethane combusts in air according to the balanced equation 2 C₂H₆(g) + 7 O₂(g) → 4 CO₂(g) + 6 H₂O(g). Starting with exactly 1.00 mol of C₂H₆, use the mole ratio of O₂ : C₂H₆ from the balanced equation to determine how many moles of O₂ are required.
gc.why: Stoichiometric ratio = 7 mol O₂ / 2 mol C₂H₆ = 3.5. So 1.00 mol C₂H₆ needs 1.00 × 3.5 = 3.5 mol O₂. Forgetting to halve the ratio gives the 7.0 trap; reading 7:2 inverted gives 3.0 or 2.0.

gc.q: Uranium-238 (²³⁸₉₂U) undergoes alpha decay, emitting an α particle (⁴₂He nucleus). Alpha decay reduces mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2. The resulting daughter nuclide is determined by ²³⁸₉₂U → α + ⁴⁻ᵐZ. Which is the daughter?
gc.why: Alpha decay: A decreases by 4 (238 → 234), Z decreases by 2 (92 → 90). Z = 90 is thorium, so the daughter is ²³⁴₉₀Th. Forgetting to change Z gives ²³⁴U; β decay (Z+1) gives ²³⁴Pa instead.

gc.q: A beaker holds pure deionized water at 25 °C and 1 atm with no dissolved acids or bases. Water self-ionizes as 2 H2O ⇌ H3O+ + OH- with Kw = 1.0x10^(-14), so [H+] = [OH-] = 1.0x10^(-7) M. Using pH = -log[H+], what is the pH of pure water?
gc.why: [H+] = 1.0x10^(-7) M, so pH = -log(10^(-7)) = 7.0. Note that pH = 7 is neutral only at 25 °C; at higher T, Kw is larger and neutral pH is below 7.

gc.q: Three initial-rate experiments at 25°C give: trial 1 [A]=1.0, [B]=1.0, rate = 0.10 M/s; trial 2 [A]=2.0, [B]=1.0, rate = 0.40 M/s; trial 3 [A]=1.0, [B]=2.0, rate = 0.10 M/s. Compare ratios to deduce the orders, then write the rate law.
gc.why: Trials 1 vs 2 ([A] doubles, rate x4) give order 2 in A. Trials 1 vs 3 ([B] doubles, rate unchanged) give order 0 in B. So rate = k[A]^2.

gc.q: A 1.00 m aqueous solution of KCl (which dissociates completely into K⁺ and Cl⁻, so van't Hoff factor i = 2) is prepared. Pure water freezes at 0.00°C with Kf = 1.86°C·kg/mol. Using ΔTf = i·Kf·m, what is the freezing point of this solution?
gc.why: ΔTf = (2)(1.86)(1.00) = 3.72°C. New Tf = 0.00 − 3.72 = −3.72°C. Forgetting i = 2 (treating KCl as a nonelectrolyte) gives −1.86°C; using i = 3 gives −5.58.

gc.q: A chemist titrates 25.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl with 0.10 M NaOH at 25 °C, reaching the equivalence point at pH = 7.0. The pH jumps very steeply across this point (from ~3 to ~11). Which acid–base indicator's color-change range is best centered on the equivalence-point pH?
gc.why: Bromothymol blue (6.0–7.6) brackets pH 7, exactly the SA+SB equivalence-point pH. Although phenolphthalein is also acceptable for SA+SB titrations because of the steep jump, BTB is the best-centered choice.

bio.q: A pond freezes from the surface downward each winter, and aquatic life survives beneath the ice layer. Which physical property of water, uniquely tied to its molecular geometry, best explains why solid water (ice) is less dense than liquid water?
opts: High specific heat capacity that buffers temperature changes
Strong cohesive forces and surface tension between water molecules
Water's universal solvent property, which prevents close packing of molecules
Hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open lattice that spaces molecules apart
The polar O-H bonds, which orient toward charged ions in solution
bio.why: Water molecules form four hydrogen bonds in ice, locking into a tetrahedral hexagonal lattice with empty space between molecules. In liquid water, hydrogen bonds break and reform, allowing closer packing, so liquid water is denser than ice. This unusual property allows ice to float and insulate aquatic ecosystems.

bio.q: Adult human hemoglobin contains two α-globin polypeptides and two β-globin polypeptides, each with its own folded heme-binding pocket. The four chains assemble into a functional oxygen-transport protein. Which level of protein structure does this multi-subunit assembly represent?
opts: Primary, the linear amino acid sequence of one chain
Secondary, repeating α-helix and β-sheet motifs within each subunit
Tertiary, the 3D fold of a single polypeptide chain
Quaternary, the assembly of two or more separately folded polypeptide subunits
bio.why: Quaternary structure refers to the spatial arrangement of multiple separately folded polypeptide chains (subunits) into a functional protein complex. Hemoglobin's α2β2 architecture is the textbook example. Tertiary structure describes the fold of just one chain.

bio.q: A hepatologist examines liver biopsies from two patients. Patient A is a chronic alcohol user; patient B has no history of substance use. Compared to patient B, patient A's hepatocytes show dramatic enlargement of one organelle that contains the cytochrome P450 family of enzymes. Which organelle is enlarged?
opts: Rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with ribosomes that make proteins
Nucleolus, which expands during ribosome biosynthesis
Lysosome, the site of intracellular hydrolytic digestion
Mitochondrion, where most of the cell's ATP is generated
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a site of lipid synthesis
bio.why: Smooth ER is the site of lipid biosynthesis and drug/toxin detoxification via the cytochrome P450 enzyme system. Chronic alcohol exposure induces hepatocyte smooth-ER expansion (and corresponding tolerance) as the cell upregulates its detoxification machinery. Rough ER (with ribosomes) handles protein synthesis.

bio.q: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is converted to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. The acetyl group then enters a cyclic series of eight reactions that generate NADH, FADH2, GTP, and CO2. Where in the mitochondrion does this Krebs (citric acid) cycle take place?
opts: Outer mitochondrial membrane, which is freely permeable to small molecules
Intermembrane space, where the proton gradient accumulates during ETC flow
Mitochondrial matrix, the compartment enclosed by the inner membrane
Inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae), which houses the ETC complexes
Cytoplasm, in association with mitochondrial outer membrane proteins
bio.why: The Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix, the soluble fluid inside the inner membrane. The ETC complexes and ATP synthase are embedded in the inner membrane (cristae); pumped protons accumulate in the intermembrane space; and glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.

bio.q: Because DNA polymerase synthesizes only 5' → 3' but the two strands of DNA are antiparallel, replication of the lagging strand proceeds discontinuously. Short DNA segments are synthesized away from the fork, each starting from an RNA primer. These segments are later joined into a continuous lagging strand. What are these segments called?
opts: RNA primers, which remain in the final product
Replication errors caused by polymerase slippage
Okazaki fragments of new lagging-strand DNA
Telomeric repeats added by the enzyme telomerase
bio.why: Okazaki fragments are the short DNA segments (1-2 kb in eukaryotes) synthesized on the lagging strand. Each starts from an RNA primer made by primase, is extended by DNA polymerase, then has its primer removed and is ligated to the next fragment. The leading strand is synthesized continuously.

bio.q: Coastal regions experience smaller daily temperature swings than inland areas at the same latitude. Marine biologists attribute this thermal stability partly to a unique physical property of liquid water that resists temperature change relative to most other substances. Which property is responsible?
opts: High specific heat, so much heat shifts its temperature only a little
Density anomaly that causes ice to float and insulate the liquid below
Polarity that makes water a nearly universal solvent
Surface tension caused by hydrogen bonding at the air-water interface
bio.why: Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity (~4.18 J/g·°C), much higher than most substances, because energy must first break extensive hydrogen-bonding networks before raising kinetic energy. Large bodies of water buffer temperature swings, moderating climate near coasts.

bio.q: When a globular protein folds in aqueous solution, the polypeptide adopts the conformation that minimizes free energy. The hydrophobic effect, driven primarily by the entropy of surrounding water molecules, is one of the largest energetic contributions to folding. As a result, hydrophobic R-groups in a folded protein tend to:
opts: Face outward toward water, where they form van der Waals contacts with surrounding solvent
Form hydrogen bonds with water and remain solvent-exposed
Become charged (deprotonated) to gain solubility in water
Cluster in the protein's interior, away from water, the hydrophobic core
Distribute randomly throughout the protein with no preference
bio.why: Hydrophobic R-groups (Val, Leu, Ile, Phe, Met) cluster in the protein's interior. Burying them releases ordered water molecules that had been forming clathrate-like structures around them, a large entropy gain. Polar/charged R-groups remain on the surface to interact with water.

bio.q: A small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule that exists separately from the main chromosome and replicates autonomously is found in a microbial genome. The molecule frequently carries antibiotic-resistance genes and can transfer between cells via conjugation. Which kind of organism most commonly carries such DNA elements?
opts: Eukaryotes, where plasmids are commonly found in the nucleus
Archaea only, and never in any bacterial species
Bacteria, where plasmids often carry resistance genes
Mitochondria, which carry plasmids instead of a circular chromosome
Viruses, where plasmids serve as the entire genome
bio.why: Plasmids are extrachromosomal, circular DNA molecules characteristic of bacteria. They replicate autonomously and often carry antibiotic resistance, virulence, or metabolic genes. While yeast (eukaryotes) have plasmids, the textbook association, and the basis for cloning vectors, is bacterial.

bio.q: Hormone binding to one G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) on a cell can ultimately activate thousands of downstream protein-kinase A molecules within seconds. The signaling pathway gains enormous amplification at each step. Which mechanism best explains this signal amplification?
opts: Each activated enzyme catalytically makes many copies of the next messenger in the cascade
The original receptor binds the hormone with very high affinity, so binding is nearly permanent
The hormone diffuses back out of the cell and activates more receptors on neighboring cells
Second messengers are permanent and keep accumulating in the cytoplasm without being degraded
The hormone covalently bonds to all of the downstream target proteins at the same time
bio.why: Signaling cascades amplify because each enzyme step is catalytic. One activated GPCR can activate ~100 G proteins, each Gαs activates ~10 adenylyl cyclases, each cyclase makes ~1000 cAMP, etc. Multiplicative amplification across stages turns a single hormone-receptor binding event into a massive intracellular response.

bio.q: The Calvin cycle in chloroplasts fixes CO₂ into a 5-carbon sugar (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, RuBP), forming an unstable 6-carbon intermediate that immediately splits into two 3-carbon molecules. The enzyme catalyzing this carboxylation is the most abundant protein on Earth. Which enzyme is it?
bio.why: RuBisCO catalyzes CO₂ fixation onto RuBP, the entry step of the Calvin cycle. It accounts for roughly half of all soluble protein in plant leaves and is considered the most abundant protein on Earth. It also has a side activity (oxygenase, leading to photorespiration), which is why C4 and CAM plants have evolved to minimize this.

bio.q: Eukaryotic cells contain three nuclear RNA polymerases that transcribe distinct classes of genes. One specific polymerase synthesizes pre-mRNAs from protein-coding genes, while the other two transcribe rRNA and tRNA respectively. Which polymerase produces eukaryotic mRNA?
opts: RNA polymerase I, transcribes large rRNA genes (28S, 18S, 5.8S) in the nucleolus
RNA polymerase II, transcribes protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA, plus most snRNAs and miRNAs
RNA polymerase III, transcribes tRNAs, 5S rRNA, and small RNAs
DNA polymerase, which copies DNA, not RNA
Mitochondrial RNA polymerase, which only transcribes mitochondrial genes
bio.why: RNA Pol II transcribes protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA. Pol I makes large rRNA in the nucleolus; Pol III makes tRNAs and 5S rRNA. The Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) coordinates capping, splicing, and polyadenylation, distinguishing mRNA biogenesis from other RNA classes.

bio.q: DNA point mutations are categorized into two types based on how the substitution affects the chemical class of the base. One type substitutes within the same chemical family (e.g., A↔G), while the other type swaps between families. Which definition correctly distinguishes these two types?
opts: Transition and transversion are interchangeable terms, with no real distinction between them
Transition: purine to purine or pyrimidine to pyrimidine; transversion: purine to pyrimidine
Transversion: a change that is always silent; transition: a change that is always missense
Both types create stop codons by definition, differing only in the base that is swapped
Transition: a change that affects only RNA; transversion: a change that affects only DNA
bio.why: Transition is a purine→purine or pyrimidine→pyrimidine substitution (chemically similar). Transversion is purine→pyrimidine (or vice versa), a bigger structural change. Transitions outnumber transversions about 2:1 because they are easier to make (similar ring structure makes mispairing easier during replication).

bio.q: Eukaryotic cilia and flagella have a strikingly conserved internal structure. A cross-section under TEM reveals a characteristic arrangement of microtubule doublets surrounding a central pair, anchored to a basal body. Which microtubule arrangement defines this axoneme?
bio.why: Motile cilia and flagella have a 9+2 axoneme: nine outer microtubule doublets around two central singlets. Dynein motor arms on the doublets generate movement by sliding adjacent doublets relative to one another. Primary (non-motile) cilia have a 9+0 arrangement and serve sensory functions (e.g., Hedgehog signaling).

bio.q: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) prevents anaphase from beginning until every chromosome is properly attached to spindle fibers from opposite poles. Until that condition is satisfied, the SAC inhibits a key cell-cycle E3 ubiquitin ligase that would otherwise trigger anaphase by ubiquitinating securin and cyclin B. Which complex does the SAC inhibit?
opts: Cyclin D-CDK4, the kinase that drives progression through G1
p53, the genome guardian that responds to DNA damage
The retinoblastoma protein (Rb), which blocks G1/S progression
ATP synthase, the mitochondrial F0F1 enzyme
bio.why: The SAC inhibits APC/C^Cdc20 until all kinetochores are attached. Once attachment is complete, SAC release allows APC/C to ubiquitinate securin (whose destruction releases active separase, which cleaves cohesin) and cyclin B (mitotic exit). Loss of SAC function (e.g., Mad2 mutations) causes chromosomal instability, a hallmark of cancer.

bio.q: HIV is a retrovirus whose genome is a single-stranded RNA. After entering a host cell, the virus must convert its RNA genome into double-stranded DNA before it can integrate into the host genome and be transcribed by host machinery. Which viral enzyme catalyzes this RNA → DNA conversion?
opts: Host DNA polymerase, recruited from the nucleus
Reverse transcriptase, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase that the retrovirus brings into the cell as part of its capsid
Host ribosomes, which translate RNA into DNA
An endonuclease that cuts host DNA at random sites
Integrase, which only handles integration of the proviral DNA
bio.why: Retroviruses (HIV, HTLV, etc.) carry reverse transcriptase as a virion protein. Once in the cell, RT copies the RNA genome to DNA (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity), then makes a complementary DNA strand to form double-stranded DNA, which is integrated by the viral integrase. RT's lack of proofreading is what makes HIV mutate so rapidly. Antiretrovirals (zidovudine, tenofovir) target RT.

ochem.q: HF (pKa ~3) is roughly 47 pKa units more acidic than CH4 (pKa ~50). Both protons sit on second-row atoms. Which CARDIO factor (Charge, Atom, Resonance, Dipole/induction, Orbitals) most directly explains the dramatic difference?
opts: Atom, within the same row, F is much more electronegative than C, so F- holds the negative charge better than CH3-
ochem.why: Comparing acidity at heteroatoms in the same row, the dominant factor is the electronegativity of the atom holding negative charge. Fluoride is far better at carrying that charge than methide, making HF orders of magnitude more acidic.

ochem.q: Acetic acid, ethanol, and ethane are dissolved in DMSO. Which has the most acidic proton, and which factor makes the largest contribution to the difference in acidity?
opts: Ethane C-H; sp3 hybridization of the resulting carbanion
Ethanol O-H; electronegative oxygen stabilizes the alkoxide
Acetic acid alpha C-H; the enolate is the most stable anion
All three protons are equivalent in acidity in DMSO
Acetic acid O-H; resonance delocalizes the carboxylate
ochem.why: The answer is the acetic acid O-H, because resonance spreads the carboxylate charge over two equivalent oxygens. That delocalization is the largest single stabilizing factor among the three conjugate bases. In DMSO the pKa values are all higher than in water (acetic acid about 12, ethanol about 29, ethane far higher), but the order is the same. The tempting choice is ethanol, since oxygen is electronegative, but ethoxide keeps its charge on one oxygen with no resonance, so it is much less stable than acetate.

ochem.q: 2-methyl-2-butene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degC, then with Zn/AcOH (reductive workup). Identify the two carbonyl products formed by cleavage across the trisubstituted alkene.
opts: Acetone + acetaldehyde (the more substituted side gives a ketone; the less substituted side gives an aldehyde)
Two molecules of acetic acid (oxidative workup)
ochem.why: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C, replacing each carbon's substituents with =O. The 2-substituted side (CMe2) becomes acetone; the 3-CH(CH3) side becomes acetaldehyde. Reductive workup (Zn/AcOH or Me2S) prevents oxidation of the aldehyde.

ochem.q: tert-Butanol is heated to 90 degC in concentrated H2SO4 with no nucleophile present. The protonated alcohol loses water to form a tertiary carbocation, which loses a beta-proton in an E1 elimination. What is the principal organic product?
ochem.why: Hot concentrated H2SO4 dehydrates tertiary alcohols by E1: protonation of OH, loss of water to give a stable tertiary carbocation, then deprotonation of a beta-CH3 by the conjugate base. The tert-butyl cation has only one type of beta-H (all three CH3 groups are equivalent), so the only possible alkene is isobutylene (2-methylpropene).

ochem.q: Treating propene with one equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C in the dark gives anti addition. Identify the major product and explain the stereochemical outcome.
opts: 1,1-Dibromopropane, a geminal dibromide on one carbon
Propylene oxide, formed by ring closure
ochem.why: Br2 first forms a cyclic bromonium ion, then bromide attacks from the opposite face. The result is a vicinal dibromide with anti stereochemistry. On propene, this is 1,2-dibromopropane.

ochem.q: Aqueous-phase pKaH measurements give ammonia approximately 9.3, methylamine 10.6, dimethylamine 10.8, and trimethylamine 9.8. Based on these values, which sequence correctly orders aqueous basicity of NH3, primary, secondary, and tertiary aliphatic amines?
opts: 2 deg > 1 deg > 3 deg > NH3 in water; gas-phase order is 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg
3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg > NH3 regardless of phase
1 deg > NH3 > 2 deg > 3 deg in water
ochem.why:
In water the order is secondary > primary > tertiary > ammonia; in the gas phase it is tertiary > secondary > primary.
The given pKaH values put dimethylamine (10.8) just above methylamine (10.6), then trimethylamine (9.8), then ammonia (9.3). Alkyl groups donate electron density and stabilize the ammonium ion, which alone would make tertiary amines strongest, as seen in the gas phase. In water, the protonated amine is also stabilized by hydrogen bonds from its N-H bonds, and a protonated tertiary amine has only one N-H, so it is solvated worst and drops below primary. The tempting choice, tertiary > secondary > primary in all phases, ignores this solvation effect.

ochem.q: Benzene is nitrated with a 1:1 mixture of concentrated HNO3 and concentrated H2SO4 at 50 degC. The active electrophile generated in situ is the nitronium ion (NO2+). What is the major aromatic product?
ochem.why: H2SO4 protonates HNO3 and dehydrates it to NO2+, the nitronium ion electrophile. Benzene attacks NO2+, forms a Wheland intermediate, and loses H+ to rearomatize, giving nitrobenzene. The aromatic ring is preserved (so no nitrocyclohexane), and the nitro group strongly deactivates the ring against further nitration under these conditions.

opts: 1 arrow: the arene π bond attacks Br2 directly, no catalyst
3 arrows: arene π to Br, Br-Br to FeBr3, FeBr3 to Br
2 steps: a Br lone pair attacks FeBr3 to form the Br2-FeBr3 complex, then the arene pi bond attacks the Br farther from Fe as the Br-Br bond breaks
No arrows, since the bromination is a radical chain
2 arrows: Br+ to the arene π bond, then FeBr3 to Br-Br
ochem.why: The answer is a two-step picture: activation of Br2 by FeBr3, then attack by the ring. First, a lone pair on one bromine attacks the empty orbital on iron, making the far bromine strongly electrophilic (Br+ like). Second, the arene pi bond attacks that bromine while the Br-Br bond breaks toward FeBr3, giving the sigma complex and FeBr4-; a base then removes the ring proton to restore aromaticity. The tempting one-arrow choice is wrong because benzene is not nucleophilic enough to attack Br2 without the Lewis acid.

ochem.q: Acetophenone (PhCOCH3) is heated with one equivalent of methylamine (a primary amine) in benzene with catalytic AcOH and a Dean-Stark trap to remove water. Identify the major product.
opts: Imine (Schiff base): PhC(=NMe)CH3, formed by condensation and loss of H2O
ochem.why: Primary amines have two N-H bonds. After nucleophilic addition gives the hemiaminal, water is eliminated and the second N-H is lost to give a neutral C=N (imine, Schiff base). Secondary amines instead form enamines.

ochem.q: Two miscible liquids in a binary mixture have boiling points of 65 degrees C and 100 degrees C. Considering vapor-pressure differences with temperature, which technique is most appropriate for separating them based on the boiling-point difference?
opts: Distillation, simple or fractional depending on the boiling-point gap
ochem.why: Distillation separates miscible liquids using their differing vapor pressures. A 35 degree gap usually allows simple distillation, but fractional distillation is preferred for narrower gaps or when high purity is required.

ochem.q: A chemist performs Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene using tert-butyl chloride and AlCl3 to make tert-butylbenzene. The reaction works in good yield. However, when the same chemist attempts the same reaction on nitrobenzene, no product forms even after extended heating. Which factor best explains the failure?
opts: The nitro group strongly deactivates the ring (resonance withdrawal); the resulting arenium intermediate cannot form
The nitro group reacts preferentially with AlCl3, consuming the Lewis acid
Friedel-Crafts alkylation requires alkenes, not alkyl halides
tert-butyl cation rearranges before substitution can occur
ochem.why: Nitro is a strong −M deactivator. It depletes electron density from the ring and destabilizes the arenium (sigma-complex) intermediate so much that Friedel-Crafts alkylation effectively fails.

ochem.q: Solvolysis of 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane in 80% aqueous acetone follows rate = k[RX], with no dependence on added nucleophile. Which step controls the rate of this SN1 process?
opts: Ionization of the C-Cl bond to a 3° carbocation
Backside attack of water on the alkyl halide
Concerted loss of HCl across the C-C bond
Capture of the carbocation by water as nucleophile
Migration of a methyl group across the C-C bond
ochem.why:
The rate-limiting step is ionization of the C-Cl bond to a tertiary carbocation.
A rate law of k[RX] means only the substrate is in the slow step. The C-Cl bond breaks to give a planar tertiary cation, and water then traps it quickly. Any hydride shift in this cation just gives an identical tertiary cation, so it does not change the product. Capture by water is the tempting wrong answer, but it happens after the slow step, which is why water does not appear in the rate law.

ochem.q: A neat-film IR spectrum of an unknown shows a sharp, strong absorption near 1715 cm^-1 with no broad O-H feature above 3000 cm^-1 and no aldehydic C-H near 2720 cm^-1. Which functional group best explains the 1715 cm^-1 band?
opts: C identical C of an alkyne
ochem.why: Saturated ketone C=O stretches absorb near 1715 cm^-1 with strong, sharp character. The absence of a broad O-H band rules out an acid, and the lack of the aldehydic C-H 'doublet' near 2720/2820 cm^-1 rules out an aldehyde, leaving a ketone.

ochem.q: Consider (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane. Each carbon bears H, CH3, Br, and a different second carbon, so each is a CIP stereocenter. How many stereocenters does the molecule have?
ochem.why: Carbons 2 and 3 each carry four different substituents (H, CH3, Br, and a different remaining group), so they are independent stereocenters. The molecule has two even though it is meso.

ochem.q: 1-Bromopropane is to be converted into 1-propanol in one step via a SN2 process at the primary carbon, with no rearrangement. Which reagent provides the cleanest result?
ochem.why: Aqueous hydroxide is a strong nucleophile but not bulky, so it executes SN2 on a primary substrate cleanly to give 1-propanol. Sodium methoxide is also a good nucleophile but would give the methyl ether instead. PCC oxidizes alcohols; HCl would not displace bromide.
